messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram gives the jug a look, then a nod, and lays a silver piece on the table. "Separate tabs. Ale, and whatever's hot in the kitchen that doesn't need a knife to eat."

He takes a pull from the cup before he goes on. "I came up the Coast Way from Nashkel. Paid off there three days back, and the road's no place to sit idle, so I'm looking for another caravan that needs a man who knows wagons and doesn't complain about the cold. If the Burning Wizard hears of one, I'd like to know."

He glances at the other two, then back to Orla. "Anyone asking after a guard in this room, you can point them at me. And if one of these two is a sellsword, I'd rather hear it now than on the road."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I look up from the cup Orla has just set in front of me and smile, though I keep my hands flat on the table, where they can be seen.

"One tab, Orla, and let it go on mine. I'll be paying for the wine whether these two like it or not, so it's easier to keep the count in one place." I nod toward Bram, then Pell, and let my eyes rest on the satchel at Pell's hip a moment longer than is polite. "As for what brings me here: I walked down from Baldur's Gate, and I'm told the Friendly Arm has work for anyone who can stand a long day on the road. I'd rather hear from someone who's been out there than from the broadsheets." I turn the cup a quarter-turn on the wood. "What about you two? You didn't all come in by the same door, and I'd wager none of you walked in off the Gate road."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
"Three tabs," I say, and set a few coppers on the table. "I pay for my own drink. Nobody buys me anything in a town I don't know yet."

I keep my hand near the satchel while I say it, and my eyes move over Bram's shield, then Sefa's boots, the dust on her hem from the road. "I came in by the High Hedge road. Work, if there is any. I hear the carters talk about hired hands, and the Friendly Arm's full of people who want paying for things they won't name." I nod at Orla. "Are the sellswords at the back in the Fist, or just wearing its look?"

scenes.narration:
Orla takes the silver without looking at it, and the coppers without looking at those either. She chalks three lines on the slate behind the bar, and the third runs off the edge of the board because, she says, that one will want room.

"Friendly Arm's all caravan work these days, and the caravans aren't what they were." She sets her jug on her hip. "Hendry's wagons went out of Nashkel in the spring and never came into Beregost. Nobody's been paid to walk that road since, not by anyone who paid up after. So if you're after wagons, friend, you'll find the Fist and the merchants still arguing over who pays for the men to look."

She tips her head toward the hearth. "Those two by the fire came in four days back. Said they were Fist. Fist men don't tip, and these two don't tip." She lowers her voice a half-step, which for Orla is still loud. "They've been asking about the Nashkel road too. Ask them yourself if you like, but I'd wait till they've eaten."

"Kitchen's pottage and bread tonight, and a fish pie if the fish came in off the cart. I'd have the pottage." She is already turning toward the back, the jug still in her hand, and over her shoulder: "Shout if you want a second cup. Shout if you want a third and I'll remember it."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram turns his cup slowly and watches the hearth without seeming to. "Hendry ran his wagons with six guards on the Nashkel stretch, and he didn't skimp. If nobody came in after the spring, somebody's been paid to keep quiet about it, or nobody's been left alive to ask." He sets the cup down. "I'll eat first, Orla. Pottage is fine."

He looks at the two by the fire for a long moment, the way he'd look at a wagon with a loose wheel. "Fist men who don't tip still have to sit somewhere. If they're asking about the Nashkel road, they'll want the drivers' names, and I'd like to know who else is asking."

Then, to Pell: "You came by the High Hedge. That road has bandits in the cuttings past the ford, and you'd know it if you'd seen a dead man on it. Did you see anything? Or did the road just look wrong?"

To Sefa, with a short nod: "You came down from the Gate. Wagons heading south, or anything heading north that looked like it shouldn't be?"

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I let Orla's three lines stand on the slate and don't argue the third one. The room is loud enough that I lean in a little, the way you do when you want the words to stay between the people who need them.

"Hendry's wagons," I say quietly. "Nashkel in spring, and never into Beregost. That's a long silence for a road that's supposed to be busy." I look at Bram, then Pell. "Bram, you came up from Nashkel three days back. Did you see anything on the road, or hear anything in Nashkel before you left? Anyone asking who was buying iron, or who was looking for men?"

Then I turn my cup again and glance toward the hearth, where the two men are eating in the same silence they came in with.

"And Pell, you asked whether those two are Fist or only dressed like it. I'd like to know that too. Orla says they've been asking about the same road." I smile without much warmth. "I'll tell you my own piece of it, since we're trading. I'm not here for work so much as for a debt I'd rather not talk about yet. But I walked from the Gate with my eyes open, and I'd rather sit with men who keep theirs open too."

I lift the cup, then set it down without drinking.

"Pottage, Orla, and a second cup when I've decided who's paying for it."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
"Work came my way from the Lower City, and I'm not going back the same road for a while," I say, and I turn my cup in front of me without drinking. "The High Hedge is quieter than the Coast Way. Fewer carts, fewer eyes. I came to see whether Beregost is worth the stop."

I say it easily. Then I let my gaze drift past Bram's shoulder to the hearth, where the two men sit with their backs to the room and their cloaks still on. One of them has a Fist badge on his shoulder, half-hidden under the wool, and the other keeps touching the hilt of his sword as if he'd forgotten it was there. I watch them in the dark glass of the shutter, where the reflection is clearer than the men themselves.

"Those two," I say quietly, for the table only. "They're not talking to each other much. Men who came in together and don't talk, when they've been on the road together four days, have usually had a quarrel. Or one of them is watching the door, and the other is watching him." I look back at Bram. "You said you'd tell anyone about a guard. I'd like to know what the Fist pays, and whether they pay it on the day or on the Gate's promise."

Then, to Sefa, with a faint shrug: "I've been out of the Gate a long while myself. If you want company down the Way, I'll listen to what you're carrying first."

scenes.narration:
Orla comes back with three wooden bowls of pottage, thin and hot, with barley and onion in it, and a heel of dark bread on a board. She sets them down without waiting for thanks and is gone again into the crowd.

By the fire the man with the badge has stopped eating. He heard the word Hendry, or heard the table lean in, and his spoon stays halfway to his mouth. He lowers it and says something short to his companion without turning his head. The companion, who has been touching his sword hilt all evening, takes his hand away and lays it on the bench beside him, where it can be reached from a standing start. The Fist badge on the first man's shoulder is brighter than the rest of his coat. The enamel is new, or he has polished it.

Neither of them looks at the table. Both are watching it in the dark glass of the shutter.

The badge-man pushes his bowl away, half finished, and stands. He takes his time settling his cloak, then crosses the room to the end of the bench, close enough to be heard over the hammering from the smithies.

"Which of you has been asking after Hendry's wagons?" he says. He does not look at anyone in particular. His voice is level and tired, the voice of a man who has been paid to ask questions and has not yet been paid enough to enjoy it. "Only the Fist would like to know. And the Fist has had four days of pottage to wait for an answer."

He waits, one hand resting on the back of the bench, his companion still seated and watching the door.

Bram doesn't get up. He sets his cup down on the wood and lets his hand stay near it.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I keep my hands where they are, flat on the wood beside the bowl, and I look up at him with the easy, open face the hospice taught me to wear for frightened families.

"I asked, Sergeant," I say. I don't know his rank, so I guess low and let him correct me. "Though I'm not sure 'asking' is the word for it. I only heard the name said at the bar, and I wanted to know if anyone living had seen those wagons since spring." I nod toward the bowl he left. "You've left good pottage going cold. Sit with us a moment, if you're here for the same answer. I'd rather hear it from a man who's been paid to look than from Orla's slate."

I don't reach for the satchel or the Book, and I keep my voice warm and low, pitched under the hammering so it stays at this bench.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
I don't turn around. I keep my hand on my spoon and let my eyes drift to the dark shutter, where the man's reflection stands a little too close to mine.

"Nobody at this table asked about Hendry's wagons," I say. My voice is mild, the kind a man uses when he is only passing the time. "Orla mentioned the wagons when she brought the bowls. The wagons were the first thing anyone said to us, and she said it, not us."

I finally look up at him, but only at his hands. One is on the bench. The other is at his belt, near the sword, and the fingers are relaxed in the way fingers are when they have not been asked to do anything yet.

"The badge is bright," I say. "I'd guess it's new, and I'd guess you polish it. A man who's proud of the Fist doesn't need to say so, and a man who's only been in it a month says so every time." I shrug and pick up the bread. "If the Fist wants an answer, it can ask Orla. She keeps the tab, and she remembers who asks questions."

I tear the bread, and my hand is steady while I do it. Under the table my boot has found the leg of the bench, and my weight is on the balls of my feet, ready to rise without a sound if the man's companion stands.

"What does the Fist pay for a man who knows the Nashkel road?" I ask. "I'd like to hear the figure before I hear the questions."

The badge-man doesn't sit down. He looks at Bram's hand on the table, then at the shield against the bench, and something in his shoulders eases a notch, the way a man's does when he has been handed a figure he can carry back.

"Eight silver the week for a man on the Fist roll," he says. "Ten if he can sit a horse. Paid on the day, if the captain's signed the sheet. Not on the Gate's promise, whatever the carters say." He glances at Pell, then away. "Who pays the Fist for this job is none of yours. You'll have to take that as it is."

His companion has already stood. The bench scrapes on the boards, and a cup goes over at the next table. The carter beside it shoves back out of the way and mutters into his beard. The companion's hand has found his hilt and stopped there, the blade still in its sheath.

"Not in my room," Orla calls from the bar, without looking up from the tap. "Either of you. Sit."

"Sit down," the badge-man says, flat, and does not turn his head. The companion stays on his feet a breath longer, eyes on Pell's hands, then lowers himself back onto the bench. He does not take his hand from the hilt.

The badge-man turns to Sefa. His mouth moves, not quite a smile. "Not a sergeant. Nobody's made me one yet." Then he turns back to Bram, and his voice drops. "You said you heard Hendry's name at the Friendly Arm. Then you'll want to talk to the captain, not me. I only ask the questions. I don't get to answer them."

He picks up his half-eaten bowl and sets it on the bench beside his companion, as if he means to come back to it. He doesn't sit again. He stays on his feet at the end of the table, one hand on the back of the bench, and waits.

The dark glass of the shutter gives back the whole table now: three faces, one shield, and two men who have not yet decided whether they are going to leave.

Beregost smells of coal smoke and hot iron even in here. Through the shutters comes the steady ring of hammers from the smithies along the Coast Way, and the light is going amber. The Burning Wizard's common room is filling up for the evening: carters, a pair of dusty sellswords, townsfolk with soot still on their forearms. The benches are crowded, and that is how three strangers end up at the same table.

Bram Halloway sits with his back to the wall and his shield propped against the bench, the old company mark painted over. Across from him is Sefa Marrin, a young woman just off the road from Baldur's Gate. Beside her is Pell Dunmore, a lean man from the Lower City with a healer's satchel slung at his hip. He came in by the western road and sat down so quietly that nobody heard him do it.

None of them has said a word to the others yet. Then Orla Tarnwick, the innkeeper, pushes through the crowd with a jug in one hand and three cups hooked on her fingers. She sets them down hard and looks from one face to the next.

"Last free seats in the house, and you three took them together," she says. "So: one tab or three? And what brings each of you into Beregost tonight?"

Bram doesn't get up. He sets his cup down on the wood and lets his hand stay near it.

"That was me, and I'll say so plainly, since you asked plainly," he says. "Bram Halloway. Ten years on the Trade Way, last six with Hendry's people and then with whoever paid. I let Orla's three lines stand on the slate and don't argue the third one. The room is loud enough that I lean in a little, the way you do when you want the words to stay between the people who need them.

"Hendry's wagons," I say quietly. "Nashkel in spring, and never into Beregost. That's a long silence for a road that's supposed to be busy." I look at Bram, then Pell. "Bram, you came up from Nashkel three days back. Did you see anything on the road, or hear anything in Nashkel before you left? Anyone asking who was buying iron, or who was looking for men?"

"And Pell, you asked whether those two are Fist or only dressed like it. I'd like to know that too. Orla says they've been asking about the same road." I smile without much warmth. "I'll tell you my own piece of it, since we're trading. I'm not here for work so much as for a debt I'd rather not talk about yet. I lift the cup, then set it down without drinking.

"Three tabs," I say, and set a few coppers on the table. "I pay for my own drink. Nobody buys me anything in a town I don't know yet."

I keep my hand near the satchel while I say it, and my eyes move over Bram's shield, then Sefa's boots, the dust on her hem from the road. "I came in by the High Hedge road. Work, if there is any. I hear the carters talk about hired hands, and the Friendly Arm's full of people who want paying for things they won't name." I nod at Orla. "Are the sellswords at the back in the Fist, or just wearing its look?"

"Work came my way from the Lower City, and I'm not going back the same road for a while," I say, and I turn my cup in front of me without drinking. "The High Hedge is quieter than the Coast Way. Fewer carts, fewer eyes. I came to see whether Beregost is worth the stop."

I say it easily. Then I let my gaze drift past Bram's shoulder to the hearth, where the two men sit with their backs to the room and their cloaks still on. One of them has a Fist badge on his shoulder, half-hidden under the wool, and the other keeps touching the hilt of his sword as if he'd forgotten it was there. I watch them in the dark glass of the shutter, where the reflection is clearer than the men themselves.

"Those two," I say quietly, for the table only. "They're not talking to each other much. Men who came in together and don't talk, when they've been on the road together four days, have usually had a quarrel. Or one of them is watching the door, and the other is watching him." I look back at Bram. "You said you'd tell anyone about a guard. I'd like to know what the Fist pays, and whether they pay it on the day or on the Gate's promise."

Then, to Sefa, with a faint shrug: "I've been out of the Gate a long while myself. If you want company down the Way, I'll listen to what you're carrying first."

I don't turn around. I keep my hand on my spoon and let my eyes drift to the dark shutter, where the man's reflection stands a little too close to mine.

"Nobody at this table asked about Hendry's wagons," I say. My voice is mild, the kind a man uses when he is only passing the time. "Orla mentioned the wagons when she brought the bowls. The wagons were the first thing anyone said to us, and she said it, not us."

I finally look up at him, but only at his hands. One is on the bench. The other is at his belt, near the sword, and the fingers are relaxed in the way fingers are when they have not been asked to do anything yet.

"The badge is bright," I say. "I'd guess it's new, and I'd guess you polish it. A man who's proud of the Fist doesn't need to say so, and a man who's only been in it a month says so every time." I shrug and pick up the bread. "If the Fist wants an answer, it can ask Orla. She keeps the tab, and she remembers who asks questions."

I tear the bread, and my hand is steady while I do it. Under the table my boot has found the leg of the bench, and my weight is on the balls of my feet, ready to rise without a sound if the man's companion stands.

"What does the Fist pay for a man who knows the Nashkel road?" I ask. "I'd like to hear the figure before I hear the questions."

The table was good. The scene had a real edge: two Fist men watching the glass, a badge that might be new, and a figure of eight silver on the table that nobody quite trusted. Orla was a strong presence, and her lines about the tab and the wagons gave us something to pull on.

From Pell's side, I liked that the mystery came to us through the room instead of being handed over. The Nashkel road, Hendry's wagons and the Fist's interest all surfaced in conversation, so I had something to read and no need to pry.

Two things I'd like more of next time. Pell's tells and watching are good material, but a few moments could have called for a check, especially reading the badge-man or the companion's hand on the hilt. And the scene ended before anyone had to decide what to do about the two men, which is fine for a first night but means we haven't yet committed to a direction. I'm happy to pick that up when the table is back together.

Yes, a few things. The biggest was reading the badge-man properly. I wanted to roll Insight on him, to see whether "the captain's signed the sheet" was a man repeating what he'd been told or something he actually believed. I never asked for the check, so we only have the surface.

I also wanted to see what the companion's hand was doing on his hilt. I could have made a Perception check, or simply moved my boot so I could get up without the bench scraping, and I didn't commit to either.

And I wanted a quiet word with Orla before the Fist men stood up. She's the one who keeps the tab and remembers who asks questions, and I'd have liked to know whether anyone had been paying her to remember Hendry.

Last, I'd have liked to ask Bram and Sefa something more pointed about their roads before the scene ended. I held back because I didn't want to talk over the table, but Pell would have pushed harder.

I took them to be the two other people at the table, each playing their own character: Bram Halloway, who is the one on the shield and the Nashkel wagons, and Sefa Marrin, the young woman off the Gate road. I don't know anything about who they are outside the game. The app shows me only their characters' names and what they say and do, so that is all I had to go on.

I also tried to play as if they were fully independent. Bram has his own reasons for leaving Nashkel and looking for a caravan, and Sefa has her own road and her own cup to turn. Pell has no reason to think they're in on anything with him, so I kept his suspicion aimed at the Fist men and not at them.
